analysis.one_liner: Limits the Religious Freedom Restoration Act so religious claims can't override workplace, civil rights, and health care protections.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote, despite 38 cosponsors — all Democrats plus one independent.
analysis.plain_summary: The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) of 1993 lets people claim that a law or rule burdens their religious practice, and courts have applied it to override some workplace and health care rules. This bill would say RFRA cannot be used to get around anti-discrimination laws, rules requiring employers to provide wages, benefits, or leave, child labor protections, or access to health care and health coverage. It would also stop people from using RFRA in lawsuits between two private parties — only the government could be sued under it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want protections against discrimination or employer-required benefits and leave, employees seeking health coverage including contraceptive coverage, women and LGBTQ people whose access to services has been limited by religious exemption claims, children protected by labor laws, and people with disabilities protected by the ADA.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, patients, women, and LGBTQ people

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes RFRA inapplicable to laws protecting against discrimination or promoting equal opportunity, specifically naming the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Violence Against Women Act [S2][S3].

It says RFRA cannot override rules requiring employers to provide wages, compensation, benefits including leave, or standards protecting collective workplace activity, nor protections against child labor, abuse, or exploitation [S2][S3].

It removes RFRA as a defense against any law providing access to, coverage of, or information and referrals for health care items and services — the category at issue in cases like Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, where employers claimed a religious exemption from the contraceptive coverage mandate [S2][S3].

It bars government-funded contractors and grantees from invoking RFRA to deny goods or services the government agreed to provide to program beneficiaries, and requires that a government be a party before anyone can bring a RFRA claim in court [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Religiously affiliated employers, hospitals, schools, and contractors that currently use RFRA to claim exemptions from benefit mandates, anti-discrimination suits, or providing specific health services would lose those defenses and face the same legal obligations as other employers.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows RFRA significantly: religious objectors would lose the ability to cite it against civil rights, wage and benefit, and health coverage laws, which critics argue weakens protection for religious exercise in the workplace and in government programs — the core counterargument to every version of this bill [S2][S3].

Religious institutions that have won RFRA exemptions under current case law, such as exemptions from providing contraceptive coverage to employees, would lose those exemptions and bear the cost of complying with mandates they object to on faith grounds [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is direct: workers, patients, and people facing discrimination gain enforceable rights that religious exemption claims can no longer block, while religiously affiliated employers lose defenses they currently hold. The bill draws a bright line rather than balancing case by case, which makes the outcome predictable but also means religious objectors get no exemption even in circumstances where a court might today find their burden substantial. How much that matters depends on how much weight one gives religious liberty versus third-party harm.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, joined by 27 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S3][S5].
The bill attracted 38 cosponsors — 37 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republicans [S4].

The only action ever taken on the bill was that referral; the Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Religiously affiliated employers, contractors, and others who use RFRA claims keep the legal exemptions they hold under current law; no worker or patient gained the protections the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: RFRA claimants; no one else gained

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do No Harm Act and assembled 27 original Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 38 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support but the bill never advanced past committee referral.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; controlled the markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two years before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, signaling floor-level opposition had it ever advanced.

against.name: Religious liberty advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Do No Harm Act versions in prior Congresses, arguing they would weaken RFRA protections for religious practice.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's sole Independent, with no Republican support; the bill also never moved in a committee chaired by the Democratic majority.

industries.industry: Religiously affiliated employers, hospitals, schools, and government contractors
industries.note: These institutions currently use RFRA to seek exemptions from contraceptive coverage mandates, employment discrimination claims, and obligations in government-funded programs. The bill would strip that defense, making them subject to the same benefit, civil rights, and health care rules as other employers.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and employer benefit plans
industries.note: By removing RFRA as a defense against health care access and coverage laws, the bill would make coverage mandates like contraceptive coverage harder for employers and plans to refuse, expanding covered services for enrollees while adding compliance obligations for plan sponsors.
